title: 1.5.24 Pseudocode: Largest of Three
description: Five multiple-choice questions on reading pseudocode plans: which is pseudocode, which plan is correct, and what makes a loop end. Checked instantly.

questions.question: Which of these is pseudocode?
options: set largest to a — plain English, laid out like code, no punctuation to get wrong
let largest = a;
console.log(largest);
if (a > b) { largest = a; }
questions.explanation: No semicolons, no braces, no console.log. Pseudocode is not written in any language and cannot be run.

questions.question: Plan A above is meant to find the largest of three numbers. Does it work?
options: No — it never compares b against c
No — it should compare all three at once in a single decision
Yes, but only when a is actually the largest
Yes — it starts by assuming a is largest, then replaces it whenever it finds something bigger
questions.explanation: Carrying "the largest so far" and replacing it is the standard shape. b and c each get their turn against the running answer.

questions.question: Plan B keeps asking for a password until it is correct. What guarantees it eventually ends?
options: Loops always stop on their own after enough passes
The word "until" guarantees it
The step inside the loop can change the answer being tested, so the condition can become false
Nothing does — a password loop can never be guaranteed to end
questions.explanation: Something inside the loop has to be able to change what the condition looks at. That is the same rule the broken plan in 1.5.23 violated.

questions.question: One of the two pseudocode conventions is "one instruction per line". What do you do with a line that is doing two things?
options: Add a comment explaining both
Split it into two lines
Indent it twice
Leave it — pseudocode has no rules
questions.explanation: Two rules do almost all the work: one instruction per line, and indent what is inside something else.

questions.question: Why is it useful that nothing can actually run either of these plans?
options: You are forced to check whether the thinking is right, instead of letting the machine find only the typing mistakes
It means the plans cannot contain any errors
It makes them faster to write than code, and that is the only benefit
It stops other people from stealing the algorithm
questions.explanation: Both plans come before code on purpose. A running program proves it compiles, not that the plan was sound.
